examples.title: A switch cleanup that keeps the money for declined orders
examples.summary: Merging one case into its neighbours makes the code shorter, and it still compiles. But a payment captured for a declined order is no longer refunded. This repo happens to have a model-checking unit test written for exactly this property, which also fails; the contract catches it without anyone having thought to write that test.

examples.title: A refactor believed equivalent that changes null handling
examples.summary: A nested switch was replaced by a one-line conditional. The agent that wrote it believed the two were equivalent, and every existing unit test passes. They differ on one input: a null status no longer throws.

examples.title: Logging a timestamp makes the decision unverifiable
examples.summary: Appending the current time to a reason string looks like harmless diagnostics. It makes the state machine depend on the clock, so its behaviour can no longer be proved, and the verifier refuses.

examples.title: An equivalent refactor passes without touching the contract
examples.summary: The same simplification as example 002, written with `default ->` instead of `==`. It really is equivalent, so the verifier proves it and the build passes.

examples.title: An intended change, reviewed as a one-line contract diff
examples.summary: Product asks for a clearer message when a customer cancels during payment. The developer changes the code and regenerates the contract, and the pull request shows exactly one changed outcome.

examples.title: A per-seat discount that rounds differently from the per-total one
examples.summary: The group discount is moved from the order total to the unit price, so that tickets can show what each seat cost. It reads as the same arithmetic, and the unit tests pass. The prover finds prices where the two versions differ by a few cents, over an input space of 2^96 values that no test could sweep.

examples.title: A doubled group discount, proved to change only groups
examples.summary: Product doubles the group discount from 10% to 20%. The developer declares that the change affects holds of six seats or more and nothing else, and the prover confirms it for every price and every smaller seat count. The pull request's claim becomes a checked fact.

examples.title: A new tier, written as one formula, also changes groups of six and seven
examples.summary: Product adds 20% off for eight seats or more. The developer writes it generally, a percentage per tier and one formula, and the pull request says that only eight seats or more are affected. The prover disagrees, and shows a group below eight seats whose price changed by a cent.

examples.title: A codec that loads whatever class a Kafka message names
examples.summary: To let one consumer decode messages of either family, the codec writes the Java class name into every payload and resolves it with Class.forName when reading. Round-trip tests pass. The module's capability contract now lists reflection, with the call site: the shape of the Jackson and XStream deserialization CVEs, caught without a CVE database.

examples.title: A codec setting that changes payloads but not what the module can do
examples.summary: Message properties are now written in alphabetical order, so that payloads in logs and dead-letter topics diff cleanly. The wire format changes, but the module reaches exactly the same JDK capabilities and libraries as before, and the capability contract passes untouched.

examples.title: Skipping one query in a Kafka listener strands a customer's money
examples.summary: When a payment is captured, the ticketing service counts the seats the order's hold still has before it decides. A developer removes that query: the hold was checked when the order was placed. No unit test covers the listener. The model checker finds a nine-step run across two customers, two services, Kafka and the clock after which a customer is charged, owns no seat, and the event that would have refunded them sits in a dead-letter topic.

examples.title: Deleting the hold sweeper, proved safe for every interleaving
examples.summary: The scheduled job that releases expired holds looks load-bearing: without it, seats of expired holds stay marked HELD. A developer deletes it anyway, and the model checker confirms that every safety invariant still holds in every reachable state, because the rest of the system already treats an expired hold as free.

examples.title: A "longest log wins" vote rule lets a Raft leader overwrite committed entries
examples.summary: Raft's election restriction compares the last log entry's term first and its index second. A developer rewrites it the intuitive way round: the candidate with more entries has seen more history, so index first, term to break ties. Every unit test passes. The prover finds a voter and a candidate for which the old rule refuses the vote and the new one grants it, which is the configuration in which a leader can overwrite an entry the cluster already committed.

examples.title: A leader that ignores newer terms in replies keeps serving a term the cluster has left
examples.summary: Raft's rule for every server is one line: a message from a newer term makes you a follower. A developer narrows it for leaders, reasoning that a leader learns of a new term from the new leader's heartbeats, not from replies to its own RPCs. The behavioural contract of the role machine, 52 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in exactly one of them, and that one is the deposed-leader case.

examples.title: A majority rewritten as "half, rounded up" lets two quorums miss each other
examples.summary: The property that every quorum system rests on is that two majorities always share a node. The module states it next to the code, as `2 * majority(n) > n`, and the build proves it for every cluster size with a bounded model checker. A developer simplifies `n / 2 + 1` to `(n + 1) / 2`, which agrees on every odd size the tests use. The prover answers with n = 2: two "majorities" of one node each, which need not overlap.

examples.title: A backoff cleanup that removes the overflow guard turns the delay negative
examples.summary: Exponential backoff is `min(cap, base << attempt)`, and the three lines that guard the shift against overflow look like paranoia, so a developer removes them. The module's properties file says a delay is never below the base, never above the cap, and never shorter than the previous attempt's. The prover finds an attempt count and a base for which the shift overflows into a negative delay, which a scheduler treats as "retry now", forever.

examples.title: A hybrid logical clock rewritten with max(), proved to never go backwards on any input
examples.summary: The receive rule of a hybrid logical clock has four branches; a developer rewrites it as one `max` and two conditionals. The property the clock exists for, that the new timestamp is later than both the last one and the message's and never behind the physical clock, is proved for every pair of 64-bit timestamps and every wall-clock reading. The refactor is merged on the strength of the proof, not of a review of the branches.

examples.title: A hybrid logical clock that drops one case stamps a receive before the message
examples.summary: The same rewrite as example 017, with the case where the last timestamp and the message share a physical part collapsed into the other two: continue whichever counter is checked first. The property that a receive event's timestamp is later than the message's is refuted with a message whose counter is ahead of the clock's. A transaction stamped with that clock would be ordered before an event it causally follows.

examples.title: Adding jitter inside the backoff kernel gives a pure module a random number generator
examples.summary: The kernels in this module are pure so that a deterministic simulator can drive the whole cluster through thousands of seeded runs and replay any failure exactly. A developer adds jitter to the backoff, the textbook improvement, by calling `ThreadLocalRandom` inside the kernel, and updates the tests to accept a range. The module's capability contract, which lists every JDK capability its bytecode can reach, gains `randomness`, and the build fails: the module can no longer be replayed.

examples.title: A 2PC coordinator that presumes commit on timeout splits the participants
examples.summary: When the vote collection times out, the coordinator aborts: a participant that has not answered may have given up. A developer softens this: if every vote that did arrive was yes, the missing ones are slow, not opposed, so commit. The one-line contract diff is reviewed and approved. The model checker finds a three-step run in which a participant votes no, its vote is still in flight when the timer fires, "everyone who answered said yes" is true of nobody, and the coordinator commits a transaction that participant has already aborted.

examples.title: Aborting on the first no vote, proved safe for every interleaving of three participants
examples.summary: The coordinator used to wait for every vote before deciding, holding every participant's locks until the last straggler or the timeout. The developer makes it abort as soon as one no arrives. The regenerated contract changes in one case, the model checker runs every interleaving of three participants, the coordinator, the votes in flight and both timeouts, and every invariant holds in every state. The change is merged on a proof, not on a reviewer's mental model of the protocol.

examples.title: A skew-tolerant tie-break for last-writer-wins lets replicas keep different values
examples.summary: Last-writer-wins resolution must be a total order on writes, or replicas that see the same two writes in different orders keep different values forever. The module states this as a law: `winner(a, b) == 1 - winner(b, a)` for distinct writes. A developer makes the tie-break tolerate clock skew, treating timestamps within five milliseconds as simultaneous and letting the node id decide. The prover finds two writes from the same node a couple of milliseconds apart that each replica resolves in favour of the one it saw first.
